sections.heading: What is naproxen used for?
sections.body:
Naproxen is a painkiller that also treats inflammation, and it belongs to the group of medicines called NSAIDs. The NHS says paracetamol is usually the best treatment for most types of pain, but naproxen is better for some types, such as period pain or back pain. It can also help with joint and muscle pain, gout, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, sprains and strains.

Naproxen comes as tablets or a liquid that is swallowed. Some types can be bought from pharmacies and others are prescribed. Adults and teenagers aged 15 and over can buy it from a pharmacy for period pain. MedlinePlus, a US source, says prescription naproxen treats osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. It says non-prescription naproxen is used for fever and mild pain such as headaches, muscle aches, menstrual pain, colds, toothaches and backaches.

sections.heading: How does naproxen work and how quickly?
sections.body:
Naproxen is an NSAID, and it works by reducing hormones that cause inflammation and pain in the body. The NHS says this reduces swelling and pain in joints and muscles. People usually start to feel better about 1 hour after taking it. With regular use it can take up to 3 days to work properly.

The NHS advises that the lowest amount that controls symptoms is used for the shortest possible time. A UK patient leaflet says naproxen should preferably be taken with or after food.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of naproxen?
sections.body:
The NHS lists constipation or diarrhoea, dizziness, feeling sleepy or tired, bloating and stomach pain, headaches, feeling or being sick, a rash and ringing in the ears as common side effects. 

Naproxen can cause an ulcer in the stomach or gut, especially after long use or in big doses. Vomiting blood or dark particles that look like coffee grounds, blood in the poo or black poo that looks like tar can be signs of bleeding in the stomach or gut. The NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 now if these happen.

A serious allergic reaction is rare, but sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or very fast or difficult breathing, needs a 999 call. Chest pain, which could be a heart attack, also needs a 999 call. The NHS also says to call 999 or go to A&E for possible aseptic meningitis, with fever, sickness, confusion, headache, neck stiffness and sensitivity to light.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with naproxen?
sections.body:
The NHS says naproxen is not suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to, or a serious side effect from, naproxen, ibuprofen, aspirin or another NSAID. A doctor may advise against it for someone who has or has had a stomach ulcer. The NHS lists conditions such as high blood pressure, severe liver or kidney failure, severe heart failure and other heart problems, Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, lupus and blood-clotting disorders among those that may rule naproxen out or call for a doctor's check.

 MedlinePlus says older adults usually take lower doses for short periods.

sections.heading: Naproxen with other medicines, alcohol and in pregnancy
sections.body:
The NHS says naproxen should not be taken at the same time as other NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or aspirin, because this raises the risk of serious side effects such as stomach ulcers. It can also interact with anticoagulants such as warfarin, steroid medicines, antidepressants and medicines to lower blood pressure. 

The NHS says people can drink alcohol while taking naproxen, but limiting it is advised because alcohol can increase the risk of stomach ulcers or bleeding. In pregnancy, naproxen is not usually recommended because it may affect the baby, in particular their circulation and the level of amniotic fluid. The NHS advises avoiding naproxen in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist advises it. Naproxen passes into breast milk in small amounts, and the NHS says it is not usually recommended while breastfeeding. Large amounts or long use of anti-inflammatories like naproxen can affect ovulation, which may make it harder to get pregnant.

faqs.q: Is naproxen the same as ibuprofen?
faqs.a: Both are NSAIDs, a group of painkillers that also reduce inflammation. The NHS advises against taking naproxen at the same time as another NSAID such as ibuprofen or aspirin. This is because it raises the risk of serious side effects such as stomach ulcers.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking naproxen?
faqs.a: The NHS says people can drink alcohol while taking naproxen. It advises limiting how much, because alcohol can increase the risk of side effects such as stomach ulcers or bleeding.

faqs.q: Does naproxen affect driving?
faqs.a: The NHS says naproxen will not usually affect the ability to drive, ride a bike or use machinery. If someone feels dizzy or tired or has problems with their vision after taking it, the NHS advises waiting until these effects have gone before driving.

faqs.q: Can I take naproxen in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says naproxen is not usually recommended in pregnancy because it may affect the baby, in particular their circulation and amniotic fluid levels. The NHS says paracetamol is usually the best painkiller in pregnancy.

faqs.q: When should I get urgent help with naproxen side effects?
faqs.a: Call 999 for sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, trouble breathing or chest pain. For vomiting blood, blood in the poo or black tar-like poo, the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 now.

diclofenac.name: Diclofenac
diclofenac.summary: Diclofenac is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that eases pain and swelling in problems affecting joints, muscles and bones. It comes as tablets, capsules, suppositories, gels, plasters and patches. Like other NSAIDs it can irritate the stomach, and long-term or high-amount use carries small risks to the heart, circulation and kidneys, so it is not suitable for everyone.

Migraines and pain after dental surgery
Gel, patches and plasters for joint pain, used on the area of the body that hurts
Children may be prescribed diclofenac for joint problems, with the type depending on their age

cautions: Not suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to diclofenac, aspirin or other NSAIDs

The NHS says diclofenac can be taken with paracetamol or codeine, but aspirin, ibuprofen or naproxen should not be combined with it without talking to a doctor

sections.heading: What is diclofenac used for?
sections.body: Diclofenac is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, or NSAID, which means it reduces swelling and pain. The NHS describes it as a treatment for aches and pains, and for problems with joints, muscles and bones. These include arthritis, sprains, back pain, migraines and pain after dental surgery. Diclofenac comes as tablets, capsules, suppositories, gels, plasters and patches. The NHS says gels, patches and plasters are used for joint pain in a particular area of the body. Children may be prescribed diclofenac for joint problems, with the type depending on their age.

sections.heading: How does diclofenac work, and how quickly?
sections.body: Diclofenac works by reducing hormones that cause inflammation and pain in the body. Tablets and capsules take about 20 to 30 minutes to start working. Gels, plasters and patches usually take 1 to 2 days. A gel, plaster or patch only works on the area where it is put on, and the NHS describes gels as treatment for pain in one area. For tablets and capsules the NHS advice is the lowest amount that works for the shortest possible time.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of diclofenac?
sections.body: Feeling sick and stomach ache are common, and the NHS advises taking tablets with a meal or snack, or just after eating. With gels, skin reactions where the gel is applied are the most common problem. The NHS describes options for irritated skin that include using the gel less often or leaving it off until the irritation settles, and says to speak to a doctor if it does not go away. Black poo, or yellowing of the skin or eyes, are warning signs, and prompt advice from a GP or NHS 111 is the route to take. Breathlessness with swollen legs can be a sign of heart failure and also needs prompt advice from a GP or NHS 111. Chest pain or symptoms of a stroke need an emergency call to 999. Swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue or throat can be a serious allergic reaction, and this also needs an immediate 999 call.

sections.heading: Heart, circulation and stomach cautions
sections.body: MedlinePlus says NSAIDs other than aspirin may have a higher risk of heart attack or stroke than not using them. UK product information says the risk of artery-clotting events such as heart attack or stroke may rise with higher amounts and longer use. The NHS lists high blood pressure and heart failure among reasons diclofenac may not be suitable. UK product information for diclofenac also lists established heart failure, ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease and cerebrovascular disease as contraindications. The NHS says tablets and capsules can cause an ulcer in the stomach or gut after long use or in big amounts, and MedlinePlus says NSAIDs may cause ulcers, bleeding or holes in the stomach or intestine. There is also a small risk of heart failure or kidney failure with the maximum amount taken for a long time.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, other medicines and alcohol
sections.body: The NHS says diclofenac is not usually recommended in pregnancy, and a doctor may advise it only if the benefits outweigh the risks. The NHS says it can be used while breastfeeding, because only tiny amounts reach breast milk. The NHS says some antibiotics, anticoagulants such as warfarin, digoxin and blood pressure medicines need caution with diclofenac. It says diclofenac can be taken with paracetamol or codeine, but aspirin, ibuprofen or naproxen should not be combined with it without talking to a doctor. There is not enough information to show that herbal remedies and supplements are compatible with it. The NHS says drinking alcohol within the national guidelines is possible, but too much may irritate the stomach and raises the risk of an ulcer.

faqs.q: Does diclofenac gel work as fast as tablets?
faqs.a: The NHS says tablets and capsules take 20 to 30 minutes to work, while gels, plasters and patches usually take 1 to 2 days. A gel, plaster or patch only works on the area where it is put on.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking diclofenac?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol within the national guidelines is possible, but drinking too much may irritate the stomach. This raises the risk of a stomach ulcer, so a pharmacist or GP can advise if there are doubts.

faqs.q: Can diclofenac be taken with other painkillers?
faqs.a: The NHS says it can be taken with paracetamol or codeine. Aspirin, ibuprofen or naproxen should not be combined with it without talking to a doctor first.

faqs.q: Is long-term diclofenac a concern for the heart?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is a small risk of heart failure or kidney failure with the maximum amount taken for a long time. Anyone with chest pain or stroke symptoms needs an emergency call to 999.

faqs.q: Can diclofenac be used in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says diclofenac is not usually recommended in pregnancy, and a doctor may advise it only if the benefits outweigh the risks. The NHS says it can be used while breastfeeding, because only tiny amounts reach breast milk.

sections.heading: What is lansoprazole used for?
sections.body: Lansoprazole is a medicine that lowers the amount of acid made in the stomach. The NHS says it is used for indigestion, heartburn, reflux disease and stomach ulcers, and occasionally for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Reflux disease is the name for stomach acid repeatedly flowing back up into the gullet. It comes as capsules and as orodispersible tablets, which are made to disperse in the mouth.

sections.heading: How does lansoprazole work, and how quickly?
sections.body: Lansoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that reduces stomach acid. The NHS says symptoms usually start to improve within 2 to 3 days. It may take up to 4 weeks for lansoprazole to work fully, so some symptoms may remain during this time.

sections.heading: What are the side effects?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headache, feeling sick and diarrhoea among the common side effects. They tend to be mild and go away when the medicine is stopped.

Serious side effects are rare, affecting fewer than 1 in 1,000 people according to the NHS. Worsening stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or dark urine can signal inflammation of the pancreas or liver. Joint pain with a red rash on sun-exposed skin can signal a skin form of lupus. Severe or persistent diarrhoea can signal an inflamed bowel. Any of these needs prompt contact with a GP or NHS 111.

A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is rare. Swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing, a tight throat, trouble swallowing, blue, grey or pale skin or lips, sudden confusion or fainting needs a 999 call straight away.

sections.heading: Taking lansoprazole with other medicines, alcohol and contraception
sections.body:
The NHS says antacids can affect how much lansoprazole the body takes in, and St John's wort may stop it working as well as it should. Medicines that can interact include warfarin, methotrexate, digoxin, tacrolimus, itraconazole, ketoconazole, theophylline and some HIV medicines. The NHS says there is not enough information to say that other complementary medicines and herbal remedies are fine to take with it.

The NHS says alcohol can make the stomach produce more acid than normal, which can irritate the lining and make symptoms worse.

The NHS says lansoprazole may make the emergency contraceptive ellaOne less effective. Regular contraceptive pills are not affected, although vomiting or severe diarrhoea can stop a pill working.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and what about long-term use?
sections.body:
The NHS advises telling a doctor first about a past allergic reaction, liver problems, low vitamin B12, an upcoming endoscopy, pregnancy or breastfeeding. Lansoprazole may hide some of the problems that would usually be found during an endoscopy.

In pregnancy the NHS says omeprazole is usually offered instead of lansoprazole. For breastfeeding, a doctor will usually recommend omeprazole or pantoprazole instead. The NHS says there is no evidence that lansoprazole affects fertility.

Taking lansoprazole for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures and gut infections. If it is taken for more than 3 months, blood magnesium may fall, causing tiredness, confusion, dizziness, muscle twitches, shaking or an irregular heartbeat, which needs contact with a doctor or NHS 111. A doctor should check regularly on people who continue it.

faqs.q: How long does lansoprazole take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says symptoms usually start to improve within 2 to 3 days. It may take up to 4 weeks to work fully, so some symptoms may remain during this time.

faqs.q: Does alcohol affect lansoprazole?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can make the stomach produce more acid than normal. This can irritate the stomach lining and make symptoms worse.

faqs.q: What about long-term use?
faqs.a: The NHS says use for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures and gut infections, and blood magnesium may fall after more than 3 months. A doctor should check regularly on people who continue it.

faqs.q: Does lansoprazole affect the contraceptive pill?
faqs.a: The NHS says regular contraceptive pills are not affected. Vomiting or severe diarrhoea can stop a pill working, and lansoprazole may make the emergency contraceptive ellaOne less effective.

faqs.q: What about pregnancy and breastfeeding?
faqs.a: In pregnancy the NHS says omeprazole is usually offered instead of lansoprazole. For breastfeeding, a doctor will usually recommend omeprazole or pantoprazole instead.

esomeprazole.name: Esomeprazole
esomeprazole.summary: Esomeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that lowers the amount of acid the stomach makes. It is used for heartburn, acid reflux and to prevent or treat stomach ulcers. The NHS advises taking proton pump inhibitors for the shortest time possible, as longer use raises the chance of some side effects.
usedFor: Heartburn and acid reflux (gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD).
Preventing and treating stomach ulcers.
Preventing ulcers in people at risk who take NSAID painkillers, as UK prescribing information (emc) describes.
Sometimes used for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
The pharmacy brand Nexium Control is for the short-term treatment of reflux symptoms such as heartburn and acid regurgitation in adults.
esomeprazole.howItWorks: Esomeprazole belongs to the proton pump inhibitor group of medicines. It reduces the amount of acid that the stomach produces. Proton pump inhibitors do this by blocking the acid-producing pumps in the stomach lining.
esomeprazole.onset: The NHS says esomeprazole starts working within 2 to 3 days, but it can take up to 4 weeks to work fully.

common: Headaches, feeling sick, diarrhoea, constipation, stomach pain and wind are common, affecting more than 1 in 100 people.
The NHS describes side effects as usually mild.
Occasionally it can cause dizziness, sleepiness or blurred vision, and the NHS advises not to drive, cycle or use machinery or tools until feeling better.
serious: Yellowing of the skin, pale stools or dark urine can signal liver problems; the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away.
Joint pain together with a red skin rash, especially on parts of the body exposed to the sun, can point to a rare form of lupus; the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away.
The NHS says to talk to a doctor if diarrhoea does not get better.
A severe allergic reaction is an emergency, and the NHS advises calling 999.
Taking it for more than 3 months may lower the level of magnesium in the blood.
Taking it for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures, gut infections and vitamin B12 deficiency.

cautions: Most adults can take esomeprazole; children should have it only if a doctor prescribes it.
The NHS lists liver problems, an upcoming endoscopy, unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting, blood in vomit or stools, and swallowing problems as things to raise with a doctor before taking it.
UK emc patient leaflets list an allergy to esomeprazole or other proton pump inhibitors, and severe liver or severe kidney problems, among the reasons for caution before taking it.
Medicines that can interact include digoxin, cilostazol, some antifungals, methotrexate, HIV medicines, phenytoin and rifampicin.
The NHS advises not taking the herbal remedy St John's wort with it.
UK emc patient leaflets say not to take esomeprazole with a medicine containing nelfinavir, an HIV medicine.
UK leaflets ask people to tell their doctor about any medicines they buy without a prescription.
The NHS says there is little information about esomeprazole in pregnancy, so it is not recommended, and doctors may propose omeprazole instead because more safety information exists for it.

The NHS says some esomeprazole passes into breast milk, probably in too small an amount to be harmful, and that a person may be able to take it while breastfeeding after checking with a doctor first; UK emc leaflets say it is not known whether it passes into breast milk and that it should not be taken when breastfeeding.

sections.heading: What is esomeprazole used for?
sections.body:
Esomeprazole is a medicine that lowers the amount of acid in the stomach. The NHS lists heartburn, acid reflux and the prevention or treatment of stomach ulcers as its uses. Acid reflux is also called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD. It is sometimes used for Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. UK prescribing information (emc) adds that it can be used to prevent ulcers in people at risk who take NSAID painkillers.

In the UK, esomeprazole is sold under brand names such as Nexium and, in pharmacies, as Nexium Control. Nexium Control is for the short-term treatment of reflux symptoms such as heartburn and acid regurgitation in adults. Children should have esomeprazole only if a doctor prescribes it.

sections.heading: How does esomeprazole work, and how quickly?
sections.body:
Esomeprazole belongs to a group of medicines called proton pump inhibitors, or PPIs. These medicines reduce the amount of acid that the stomach produces. They do this by blocking the acid-producing pumps in the stomach lining.

The NHS says esomeprazole starts working within 2 to 3 days. It can take up to 4 weeks to work fully. Esomeprazole is made as gastro-resistant tablets and capsules, as granules for making up into a liquid, and as a form for injection or infusion.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of esomeprazole?
sections.body:
The NHS describes side effects of esomeprazole as usually mild. Common ones, affecting more than 1 in 100 people, include headaches, feeling sick, diarrhoea, constipation, stomach pain and wind. Occasionally it can cause dizziness, sleepiness or blurred vision. If this happens, the NHS advises not to drive, cycle or use machinery or tools until feeling better.

Some side effects are serious. Yellowing of the skin, pale stools or dark urine can signal liver problems. Joint pain with a red skin rash on parts of the body exposed to the sun can point to a rare form of lupus. Diarrhoea that does not get better is a reason to talk to a doctor. For the liver and lupus signs, the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away. A severe allergic reaction is an emergency, and the NHS advises calling 999.

sections.heading: Esomeprazole with other medicines and herbal remedies
sections.body: Some medicines can interact with esomeprazole. The NHS names digoxin, cilostazol, some antifungals, methotrexate, HIV medicines, phenytoin and rifampicin as examples. It advises not taking the herbal remedy St John's wort with esomeprazole. UK emc patient leaflets say not to take esomeprazole with a medicine containing nelfinavir, an HIV medicine. UK leaflets also ask people to tell their doctor about any medicines they buy without a prescription.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with esomeprazole?
sections.body:
Most adults can take esomeprazole. The NHS lists several situations to raise with a doctor first: liver problems, an upcoming endoscopy, unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting, blood in vomit or stools, and swallowing problems. UK emc patient leaflets list an allergy to esomeprazole or other proton pump inhibitors, and severe liver or severe kidney problems, among the reasons for caution before taking it.

The NHS says there is little information about esomeprazole in pregnancy, so it is not recommended. Doctors may propose omeprazole instead, because more safety information is available for it. The NHS says some esomeprazole passes into breast milk, probably in too small an amount to be harmful, and that a person may be able to take it while breastfeeding after checking with a doctor first. UK emc leaflets say it is not known whether esomeprazole passes into breast milk and that it should not be taken when breastfeeding. The NHS says there is no evidence that esomeprazole reduces fertility in men or women.

sections.heading: Taking esomeprazole for a long time
sections.body:
The NHS notes that PPIs, like most medicines, have side effects, so it is best to take them for the shortest time possible. Taking esomeprazole for more than 3 months may lower the level of magnesium in the blood. Taking it for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures, gut infections and vitamin B12 deficiency.

After long-term use, the NHS advises speaking to a doctor first, because stopping suddenly can bring symptoms back with extra acid production. NHS guidance documents describe gradual tapering after long-term use.

faqs.q: How long does esomeprazole take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says esomeprazole starts working within 2 to 3 days. It can take up to 4 weeks to work fully.

faqs.q: Can I drive while taking esomeprazole?
faqs.a: Occasionally esomeprazole can cause dizziness, sleepiness or blurred vision. If this happens, the NHS advises not to drive, cycle or use machinery or tools until feeling better.

Taking it for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures, gut infections and vitamin B12 deficiency. A doctor decides whether long-term use is right for a person.

faqs.a: The NHS says there is little information about esomeprazole in pregnancy, so it is not recommended. Doctors may propose omeprazole instead, because more safety information is available for it. The NHS says some esomeprazole passes into breast milk, probably in too small an amount to be harmful, and that a person may be able to take it while breastfeeding after checking with a doctor first. UK emc leaflets say it is not known whether esomeprazole passes into breast milk and that it should not be taken when breastfeeding, so the advice differs between sources.

faqs.a: After long-term use, the NHS advises speaking to a doctor first, because stopping suddenly can bring symptoms back with extra acid production. NHS guidance documents describe gradual tapering after long-term use.

sections.heading: What is propranolol used for?
sections.body: Propranolol is a beta blocker. The NHS lists heart conditions, including high blood pressure, some symptoms of anxiety and the prevention of migraines among its uses. In children, NHS documents describe propranolol liquid being used for infantile haemangiomas, which are vascular birthmarks. A Dorset NHS document lists this use as off-label, meaning outside the manufacturer's licence, and restricts it to starting by a specialist. In the UK propranolol is available on prescription only, and is made as tablets, slow-release capsules and a liquid.

sections.heading: How does propranolol work, and how quickly?
sections.body: Propranolol slows the heart rate. The NHS says it usually starts to work within a few hours. For heart conditions or high blood pressure the full effect can take 2 to 3 weeks. For migraine prevention it can take several weeks to make a real difference, so the benefit is not immediate.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of propranolol?
sections.body:
The NHS says the most common side effects are usually mild and do not last long. These are feeling dizzy or tired, cold hands or feet, difficulty sleeping and nightmares. Dizziness is most likely when first starting or after an increase in dose, and the NHS says anyone affected should not drive, ride a bike or use tools or machinery. Hospital leaflets also list nausea and diarrhoea or constipation.

The NHS describes serious side effects as rare. It advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 straight away for unusual or easy bruising.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with propranolol?
sections.body:
The NHS lists several situations where propranolol may not be suitable, including a past allergic reaction to it or another medicine, low blood pressure, a slow heart rate, worsening heart failure, and lung disease or asthma. UK patient leaflets say that people who have ever had asthma or wheezing should not take propranolol tablets.

The NHS lists diabetes among the conditions to mention to the doctor, and says propranolol may make it more difficult to recognise the warning signs of low blood sugar. Leaflets say it may delay the response to treatment of low blood sugar.

On pregnancy, the NHS says propranolol can be taken but may sometimes affect a baby's growth, so extra growth scans are usually offered from around 32 weeks. The NHS says breastfeeding is acceptable if the baby is healthy, because only tiny amounts pass into breast milk. Some NHS trust migraine guidance, including from Cambridge University Hospitals, does not recommend it in pregnancy, when planning a pregnancy or during breastfeeding. The two sources therefore differ, and the clinician weighs this up for each person.

sections.heading: Taking propranolol with other medicines, alcohol and stopping
sections.body:
The NHS says that other blood pressure medicines can sometimes lower blood pressure too much, causing dizziness or fainting. Cold remedies, including pharmacy-bought ones, and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and naproxen are also listed, and the NHS says NSAIDs can raise blood pressure. The NHS says alcohol can strengthen the blood-pressure-lowering effect, which may cause dizziness or light-headedness.

The NHS describes stopping suddenly after long-term use as able to cause extra effects such as an irregular heartbeat, sweating and shaking. The prescriber normally lowers the dose gradually, and any change is decided with them.

The NHS says propranolol does not stop contraception working, but combined pills and the contraceptive patch are usually not recommended with it.

sections.heading: Long-term use and anxiety
sections.body:
The NHS says blood pressure is checked regularly for people taking propranolol long term for migraines or anxiety. For anxiety, the NHS says there do not seem to be lasting harmful effects from taking it for several months or years, and that it is best taken only for as long as needed.

Some local NHS prescribing guidance, such as the Lancashire and South Cumbria formulary, advises against starting propranolol for generalised anxiety disorder or panic disorder and warns that it can be very toxic in overdose. Anyone in immediate danger can call 999, use NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or call Samaritans free on 116 123 at any time.

faqs.q: Is propranolol used for anxiety?
faqs.a: The NHS says propranolol can help with some symptoms of anxiety. It is best taken only for as long as needed, according to the NHS. Some local NHS guidance is more cautious, so whether it suits a person is for their clinician to decide.

faqs.q: Does propranolol affect contraception?
faqs.a: The NHS says propranolol will not stop contraception working. However, the combined pill and contraceptive patch are not usually recommended with propranolol. Vomiting or prolonged diarrhoea can also make the pill less effective.

faqs.q: Can people with diabetes have propranolol?
faqs.a: The NHS lists diabetes among the conditions to tell the doctor about before starting propranolol. The medicine may make it more difficult to recognise the warning signs of low blood sugar.

faqs.q: Can people drive while taking propranolol?
faqs.a: Propranolol can make some people feel dizzy, especially when first starting or after an increase in dose. The NHS says anyone affected should not drive, ride a bike or use tools or machinery. If unsure, a doctor or pharmacist can advise.

faqs.q: What happens if propranolol is stopped suddenly?
faqs.a: The NHS describes extra effects after stopping suddenly following long-term use, such as an irregular heartbeat, sweating and shaking. The prescriber normally lowers the dose gradually, and decides how.

faqs.q: Is Inderal the same as propranolol?
faqs.a: Inderal is a UK brand name of propranolol hydrochloride tablets, made by Atnahs Pharma UK. Inderal LA is a modified-release capsule brand.

The NHS advises against driving, riding a bike or using tools or machinery until fully alert and awake if drowsy.

sections.heading: What is loratadine used for?
sections.body: Loratadine is an antihistamine that the NHS describes as non-drowsy and as relieving allergy symptoms. In the UK its licensed uses, according to the summary of product characteristics (SmPC), are the symptomatic treatment of allergic rhinitis and of chronic idiopathic urticaria. Allergic rhinitis is the medical name for hay fever and similar allergies that affect the nose, and urticaria is the medical name for hives. Chronic idiopathic urticaria means hives that last a long time without an identified cause. The NHS says loratadine can be bought from pharmacies and shops and can also be prescribed. It comes as tablets and as a liquid medicine, and the NHS gives Clarityn as the brand name. The UK medicines database (emc) holds product information for the tablets and for the syrup, both under the Clarityn Allergy name. MedlinePlus, a US source, lists loratadine (Claritin) among antihistamines that cause less sleepiness than others.

sections.heading: How does loratadine work?
sections.body: When someone meets something they are allergic to, the body releases histamine, a chemical involved in the allergic reaction. The NHS says loratadine works by blocking the effects of histamine, which reduces allergy symptoms. It eases the symptoms of an allergy rather than removing the allergy itself. The NHS says loratadine is much less likely to make people sleepy than some other antihistamines, although some people still feel slightly sleepy. Even so, the NHS lists drowsiness as the most common side effect. The NHS says people may begin to feel better within 1 to 3 hours of taking it.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of loratadine?
sections.body: Drowsiness is the most common side effect, and the NHS says trying a different non-drowsy antihistamine may help if it happens. The NHS says drowsiness happens in more than 1 in 100 people. If drowsy, the NHS advises not driving, riding a bike or using tools or machinery until fully alert and awake. The NHS says children may also get headaches. The UK patient leaflet lists headache, increased appetite and difficulty sleeping as common effects in adults and children over 12. Rarely, a person can have a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to loratadine itself. The NHS says to call 999 for sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, very fast or struggling breathing, a tight throat or trouble swallowing, skin, lips or tongue turning blue, grey or pale, sudden confusion or drowsiness, or fainting. It also says not to drive yourself to A&E in that situation. MedlinePlus, a US source, lists rash, hives, itching, trouble breathing or swallowing, or swelling of the face, lips or throat as reasons to call a doctor right away. In the UK, NHS 111 or the GP the same day is the route for urgent advice that is not an emergency. One UK patient leaflet describes dizziness and nausea as very rare effects and advises contacting a doctor if fits occur.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, breastfeeding, other medicines and alcohol
sections.body: The NHS says loratadine can be taken in pregnancy and advises checking with a pharmacist or doctor. Its antihistamines page says loratadine is usually recommended if an antihistamine is needed in pregnancy. The UK SmPC reports more than 1000 exposed outcomes showing no malformation or foetal toxicity, yet says it is preferable as a precaution to avoid loratadine in pregnancy. For breastfeeding, the NHS says only very small amounts of loratadine get into breast milk. The UK SmPC takes a more cautious line, saying loratadine is excreted in breast milk and that its use in breastfeeding women is not recommended. The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service reports that occasional cases of reduced milk supply have been described with loratadine. According to the NHS, loratadine does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception. The SmPC notes that inhibitors of the liver enzymes CYP3A4 or CYP2D6 could raise loratadine levels. The NHS says to tell a pharmacist or doctor about other medicines, including ones bought without a prescription, and names amiodarone, cimetidine, erythromycin and any medicine that causes drowsiness, dry mouth or difficulty peeing. The leaflet advises that people with rare hereditary galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take the tablets. The leaflet says the tablets have not been shown to add to the effects of an alcoholic drink, but the NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol because it can make a person sleepy. On long-term use, the NHS says loratadine is unlikely to do harm but is best taken only for as long as needed.

faqs.q: Does loratadine make you drowsy?
faqs.a: It is described as non-drowsy, because the NHS says it is much less likely to cause sleepiness than some other antihistamines. Drowsiness is still the most common side effect. The NHS advises not driving, riding a bike or using tools or machinery until fully alert if it happens, and says a different non-drowsy antihistamine may help.

faqs.q: Can loratadine be used in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says loratadine can be taken in pregnancy and advises checking with a pharmacist or doctor. The UK SmPC prefers avoiding it in pregnancy as a precaution, despite reassuring data. The NHS says only very small amounts reach breast milk, while the SmPC does not recommend its use in breastfeeding women.

faqs.q: Does loratadine affect the contraceptive pill?
faqs.a: According to the NHS, loratadine does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception. A pharmacist can answer questions about other medicines.

faqs.q: Is it harmful to take loratadine for a long time?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is unlikely to do harm if taken for a long time. It also says it is best taken only for as long as needed.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with loratadine?
faqs.a: The leaflet says loratadine has not been shown to add to the effects of an alcoholic drink. The NHS still says it is best not to drink alcohol, because it can make a person sleepy.

sections.heading: What is fexofenadine used for?
sections.body:
Fexofenadine is an antihistamine medicine that relieves the symptoms of allergies. The NHS lists hay fever, conjunctivitis, eczema, hives, insect bite and sting reactions and some food allergies among the problems it is used for. MedlinePlus describes it as treating allergy symptoms such as a runny nose, sneezing, and red, itchy or watery eyes, as well as itching and redness caused by hives.

The NHS says 180mg tablets for treating hives are available from pharmacies. MedlinePlus has a separate page for products that combine fexofenadine with pseudoephedrine, which are different products from fexofenadine on its own.

sections.heading: How does fexofenadine work?
sections.body:
Fexofenadine blocks histamine, a substance in the body that drives allergy symptoms. The NHS says that by blocking the effects of histamine it reduces the symptoms, and that people should start to feel better within 1 to 2 hours. A 2024 clinical review describes it as a non-sedating, second-generation H1 antihistamine.

The NHS classes fexofenadine as non-drowsy and says it seems less likely to cause sleepiness than other non-drowsy antihistamines. It also says fexofenadine is unlikely to cause harm when used for a long time, though it is best taken only for as long as it is needed.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of fexofenadine?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headaches, feeling sleepy, feeling sick and feeling dizzy as the common side effects. Fexofenadine is classed as a non-drowsy antihistamine, but some people still feel quite sleepy. The NHS advises not driving, cycling or using tools or machinery while feeling sleepy or dizzy. Leaflets say fexofenadine is unlikely to affect the ability to drive or use machinery, but advise checking first that the tablets do not cause sleepiness or dizziness.

Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat with difficulty breathing can be a sign of a serious allergic reaction. The leaflets say to stop the medicine and tell a doctor immediately. In an emergency, call 999.

sections.heading: Fexofenadine with food, drink and other medicines
sections.body:
The NHS says grapefruit, orange and apple juice can reduce how well fexofenadine works. MedlinePlus likewise advises taking it with water rather than with fruit juices such as orange, grapefruit or apple juice. The NHS also says it is best not to drink alcohol while taking fexofenadine, as it can make you feel sleepy.

Leaflets say that indigestion remedies containing aluminium and magnesium can lower how much fexofenadine is absorbed, and advise leaving a gap between the two. A leaflet states that apalutamide, a prostate cancer medicine, may decrease the effect of fexofenadine. The NHS says fexofenadine does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception.

sections.heading: Who can take fexofenadine, and who needs extra care?
sections.body:
The NHS says tablets for adults and children aged 12 and over can be bought from pharmacies and supermarkets, while tablets for children under 12 are only available on prescription from a doctor. The NHS lists liver or kidney problems and heart problems among the reasons fexofenadine may not be suitable, and leaflets advise talking to a doctor or pharmacist first about liver or kidney problems, heart disease or older age. One leaflet says antihistamines such as fexofenadine may cause a fast or irregular heartbeat.

The NHS lists pregnancy, trying to get pregnant and breastfeeding among the situations where fexofenadine may not be suitable. UK leaflets advise against use in pregnancy unless necessary and say it is not recommended while breastfeeding. The NHS also says anyone due an allergy test should check first, because the medicine can affect the results. The NHS lists having ever had an allergic reaction to fexofenadine or any other medicine among the reasons it may not be suitable. Leaflets differ in wording between products, so the leaflet that comes with a particular product applies to it.

faqs.q: Is fexofenadine a non-drowsy antihistamine?
faqs.a: The NHS classes fexofenadine as non-drowsy and says it seems less likely to cause sleepiness than other non-drowsy antihistamines. Even so, some people feel quite sleepy or dizzy, and the NHS advises not driving, cycling or using tools or machinery if that happens.

faqs.q: Can fruit juice be drunk with fexofenadine?
faqs.a: The NHS says grapefruit, orange and apple juice can reduce how well fexofenadine works. MedlinePlus advises taking it with water rather than fruit juice. The NHS also says it is best not to drink alcohol while taking fexofenadine.

faqs.q: How quickly does fexofenadine work?
faqs.a: The NHS says people should start to feel better within 1 to 2 hours. It says fexofenadine is unlikely to cause harm when used for a long time, but it is best taken only for as long as it is needed.

faqs.q: Can fexofenadine be bought without a prescription?
faqs.a: The NHS says tablets for adults and children aged 12 and over can be bought from pharmacies and supermarkets. Tablets for children under 12 are only available with a prescription from a doctor.

faqs.q: Does fexofenadine affect contraception?
faqs.a: The NHS says fexofenadine does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception.

faqs.q: Can fexofenadine be used in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS lists pregnancy, trying to get pregnant and breastfeeding among the situations where fexofenadine may not be suitable. UK leaflets advise against use in pregnancy unless necessary and say it is not recommended while breastfeeding. A GP or pharmacist can advise on an individual situation.

sections.heading: What are codeine and co-codamol used for?
sections.body:
Codeine is an opioid painkiller that the NHS describes as a medicine for pain, for example after an operation or injury.

Co-codamol is a combination of two painkillers, paracetamol and codeine. It is used for aches and pains, including period pain, muscle pain and toothache. The NHS says it is used when everyday painkillers such as ibuprofen, aspirin or paracetamol on their own have not worked.

The NHS says codeine is not suitable for everyone. It should not be given to children under 12, and young people aged 12 to 18 are given it only if everyday painkillers have not worked.

Product leaflets show that co-codamol comes in different strengths. The NHS says the lowest strength can be bought from a pharmacy, while higher strengths need a prescription.

sections.heading: How do codeine and co-codamol work?
sections.body:
Codeine is an opioid. The NHS says it acts on pain receptors in the central nervous system and the brain to block pain signals to the rest of the body. It also slows digestion, which is why it can cause constipation.

In co-codamol the codeine is combined with paracetamol. The NHS says co-codamol can take up to an hour to start working.

sections.heading: Side effects, constipation and dependence
sections.body:
The NHS lists constipation, feeling or being sick, and feeling sleepy as common side effects of codeine and co-codamol.

Because codeine slows digestion, the NHS suggests eating more fibre and drinking plenty of fluids for constipation. If that does not help, a laxative can be used after checking with a pharmacist or doctor, and the NHS says lactulose is usually the best choice.

The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to codeine, and advises talking to a doctor if there is a worry. It advises against stopping suddenly after regular use, and says the doctor reduces the dose gradually over weeks or months.

The NHS describes a serious allergic reaction, slow or shallow breathing, an irregular heartbeat and low blood pressure as rare serious side effects. It says to call 999 or go to A&E for breathing difficulty, a fit or allergic symptoms such as swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue.

sections.heading: Paracetamol in co-codamol and other medicines
sections.body:
Co-codamol contains paracetamol. The NHS advises against combining it with other paracetamol-containing medicines unless a doctor has said to, because of the risk of too much paracetamol. The product leaflets say cold and flu remedies are among the products to check.

The NHS says taking too much co-codamol can be harmful, and the leaflets say too much paracetamol can cause delayed, serious liver damage.

The leaflets say to get medical advice if too much has been taken, even when feeling well. A North Tees and Hartlepool NHS leaflet gives NHS 111 as the number to call, and says to call 999 or go to A&E in an emergency.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and what about pregnancy, driving and alcohol?
sections.body:
The NHS lists a lung problem, a head injury, adrenal gland problems, a condition that causes fits, an addiction to alcohol, an underactive thyroid, and kidney or liver problems among the reasons codeine may not be suitable. It also says codeine should not be given to anyone under 18 who has had their tonsils or adenoids removed because of obstructive sleep apnoea. A pharmacist or doctor can say whether it suits a particular person.

The NHS says codeine can be used during pregnancy, but long-term use is not advised. Codeine used near the end of pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in the baby, who may need extra time in hospital for observation.

The NHS says not to take codeine while breastfeeding, because small amounts reach breast milk and can cause breathing problems and drowsiness in the baby. The Specialist Pharmacy Service says the MHRA gives the same advice. A doctor or pharmacist can recommend a more suitable painkiller.

Co-codamol leaflets say it can cause dizziness or drowsiness, and not to drive or use machinery if affected. The NHS says alcohol may make a person sleepier and can raise the risk of serious side effects, and that recreational drugs such as cannabis, cocaine or heroin also raise the risk of serious side effects, including breathing difficulties.

faqs.q: Can you become addicted to codeine?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to codeine and to talk to a doctor about any worry. The NHS advises against stopping suddenly after regular use, and says the doctor reduces the dose gradually.

faqs.q: Why does codeine cause constipation?
faqs.a: The NHS says codeine slows down digestion, which is why it can cause constipation. The NHS suggests more fibre and fluids, and a laxative after checking with a pharmacist or doctor.

faqs.q: Can co-codamol be taken with other paracetamol medicines?
faqs.a: Co-codamol already contains paracetamol, and the NHS and product leaflets advise against taking other paracetamol-containing medicines with it. Cold and flu remedies are among those to check, because too much paracetamol can cause liver damage.

faqs.q: Is codeine used while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS advises against it, because small amounts of codeine pass into breast milk and can cause breathing problems and drowsiness in the baby. A doctor or pharmacist can recommend a more suitable painkiller.

faqs.q: Can you drink alcohol with co-codamol?
faqs.a: The NHS says drinking alcohol with codeine may make a person sleepier and can raise the risk of serious side effects. Co-codamol leaflets say not to drive or use machinery if drowsy or dizzy.
